title: Beyond Direct Imaging: Quantum Measurement Design for Small-Target Detection in UAV Hyperspectral Sensing
authors: Qipeng Qian, Jialiang Jin, Shihao Wang, Yuntao Qian
abstract: Small mineral patches can be spectrally distinct yet difficult to detect when diffraction mixes their light with the surrounding rock. Conventional hyperspectral detectors analyze recorded intensities, leaving an opportunity to recover target evidence through the optical measurement itself. We develop a quantum-assisted framework for exploiting this opportunity in prospective unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) hyperspectral sensing. A common radiometric and diffraction model describes direct imaging and spatial-mode measurements of the same light. The theory identifies target changes that survive background fitting and explains when mode measurements retain more detection information. It quantifies losses from mode mismatch and unresolved outputs, linking the quantum benchmark to finite receiver design. A common-basis result identifies when material spectra can share a spatial measurement at fixed geometry. An adaptive receiver uses an imaging pilot to select candidate modes and combines both stages in a full-region presence test. Simulations based on measured mineral spectra and published UAV acquisition scales demonstrate gains over complete direct imaging at a shared active-exposure budget, including pilot cost and optical loss. At matched empirical 1\% region-level false alarms, detection increases from 62.95\% to 69.65\% for a representative target. Paired analysis supports gains with registration uncertainty and, separately, under controlled nonuniform backgrounds. Calibrated mode errors reveal where measurement losses weaken or reverse the benefit. These results connect background identifiability to receiver choices and their operating conditions. They provide a framework for designing spatial measurements alongside spectral channels to detect small material features.
summary: This paper proposes a quantum-assisted framework to improve the detection of small mineral targets in UAV hyperspectral images by moving beyond simple intensity measurements. It leverages the information contained within the optical measurement itself by designing adaptive spatial-mode receivers. The results show that this quantum approach significantly boosts detection rates compared to standard direct imaging techniques under shared measurement budgets.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of detecting small, spectrally distinct mineral patches in UAV hyperspectral sensing when their light signal is mixed with the background due to diffraction.
main_result: A quantum-assisted framework was developed that demonstrates detection gains (e.g., 62.95% to 69.65%) over complete direct imaging by exploiting information encoded in the optical measurement itself.
method: The authors utilize a quantum-assisted framework based on a common radiometric and diffraction model, employing spatial-mode estimation and advanced information metrics to quantify residual target information.
model_or_system: The physical system is an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) hyperspectral imager observing a geological region. The model compares direct imaging (DI) with adaptive spatial-mode measurements to distinguish localized compositional changes from the continuous background matrix.
key_observables: Detection probability (%), information retention, quantum Chernoff Information ($C_Q$), and background-aware information metrics ($J_{Q,eff}, J_{E,eff}$).
important_parameters: Active-exposure budget, false alarm rates (1% region-level), and the spectral/spatial characteristics of the target mineral patches.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a common radiometric and diffraction model, and the quantum benchmark is linked to finite receiver design, while local tests may approximate full-scene convergence.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the comparison between Complete Direct Imaging (DI) and the Adaptive Receiver using an imaging pilot to select candidate modes. Other figures compare detection probabilities under various acquisition strategies.
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework by modeling the measurement process using coherence operators and information theory, deriving performance metrics, and then simulating and comparing the detection capabilities of different measurement strategies (DI vs. Adaptive Receiver) using measured mineral spectra.
why_interesting: Although the application is remote sensing, the core methodology involves designing optimal quantum measurements (spatial-mode selection) to extract maximum information about a localized unknown parameter (the target spectrum) from a noisy, mixed signal, which is highly relevant to quantum sensing and quantum estimation theory.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The common optical scene and two alternative acquisitions. Complete direct imaging uses the full observation budget for all image pixels and spectral channels. The adaptive receiver uses a paid imaging pilot to select eight candidate PSF modes, measures new light in those modes and their complement, and combines both records in a full-ROI presence test. Green paths carry scene light; blue paths carry recorded data, and the dashed arrow carries classical control of the mode measurement. The true target position is supplied to neither receiver.

Fig. 2. Literature-grounded scene inputs and physical scales. Measured calcite and dolomite reflectances determine the finite spectral contrast. The scale comparison distinguishes the target diameter, the 6.075-mm simulated DI pixel pitch, diffraction scale, reference-camera ground sampling, and search-ROI width. The fine DI grid represents the complete optical image; the 48.6-mm reference-camera GSD is not the sampling used by the DI baseline.

Fig. 3. From the quantum information gap to a finite optical measurement. Left: specified-position local information relative to DI after eliminating per-band brightness. Right: finite-contrast Chernoff information at d = 6.5 mm with position and brightness supplied. The reference PSF uses the actual chromatic pupil projections and a complement output. Local efficient information and finite-contrast Chernoff information answer different questions, but both show strong concentration in a small number of spatial modes.

Fig. 4. Coverage of the unknown target by eight pilot-selected candidate centers. Coverage denotes at least one candidate within 10 mm of the true center; the truth is used only for this diagnostic. The pilot uses 70% of the shared active observation and the same fixed 6.5-mm detection template for every true diameter.

Figure 4 reports whether any of the eight pilot-selected centers lies within 10 mm of the target. This descriptive alignment diagnostic uses truth only for evaluation; it neither restricts the position prior nor determines detection acceptance. Coverage rises from 66.10% at 5.5 mm to 90.25% at 6.5 mm, reaching 98.80% at 7.5 mm. Keeping separated max- ima usually supplies a useful candidate in the high-detection regime. The subsequent acquisition uses the actual orthogonal- ized fields, accounting for overlap among the original PSFs. The full-field experiment below measures whether this placement, together with the retained pilot evidence, makes the remaining mode-stage exposure useful.
